arguments.heading: Argument analysis: April 29, 2026 session
paragraphs: the sides that brought the case asked the Court to reverse the decision below. They argued that statements consistent with skinny-label use cannot count as active inducement. They contended section 271(b) permits selling dual-use products without active inducement. They invoked Twombly and Iqbal on plausibility. They disputed the opposing sides' claimed new discovery evidence. They also asserted Hatch-Waxman section viii protections. The approved record does not support additional the side that brought the case requests.

the opposing sides contested the investor-only characterization of the press releases. They cited Grokster describing advertising as a classic form of inducement. The approved record does not support additional the opposing side arguments in this session.

The United States argued inducement requires active encouragement. It said lack of discouraging disclaimers is irrelevant. It argued the Federal Circuit erred by giving any weight to a skinny label. It described its test as acts or messages showing clear intent to encourage infringement. It invoked Grokster's clear-expression standard. It said describing a product as a generic equivalent is normal. It said pairing generic Vascepa with an approved-use statement would strongly suggest inducement. It said a plaintiff must allege statements showing clear purpose to cause infringement.

The justices tested several assumptions. Justice Sotomayor tested whether the sides that brought the case need new rules and whether the complaint satisfies Twombly and Iqbal. Justice Thomas tested whether generics should state SH-only approval and whether quoting brand praise could induce infringement. [official source, official source] Justice Jackson tested the statutory sameness requirement for generic labels. Justice Gorsuch tested a website disclaimer indicating fewer than all indications. Justice Kagan tested whether the press releases were investor-oriented rather than marketing to doctors. Justice Kavanaugh tested amicus Waxman's concern about the Hatch-Waxman compromise.

the sides that brought the case answered the justices' questions. They said Hikma stated SH-only approval and no affirmative anti-infringement steps are required. They said generics cannot add disclaimers or new label language. They affirmed the statutory sameness requirement. They said the accused statements were anodyne and consistent with non-infringing use. They acknowledged quoting brand claims could plausibly state inducement if it clearly promotes infringement. They cited Grokster's distinction from Sony. They said no inducement liability arises from not adding brand-omitted label content. The approved record does not show a separate the opposing side answer to these questions.
This session was not a reargument, so no reargument changes are described. The lower court's action was granting the motion to dismiss. No outcome is predicted here.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case is about generic drug makers and patent liability. Hikma and other generic makers face claims by Amarin, which sells the brand drug Vascepa. The fight centers on whether Hikma's public statements encouraged doctors to infringe Amarin's patent.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 1, lines 1-9

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: A district court, Judge Andrews, granted a motion to dismiss the case. That means the judge threw out Amarin's complaint without a full trial. the opposing sides acknowledged this lower-court outcome during argument. The Supreme Court agreed to review the dispute.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 60, lines 29-31

sections.heading: Who argued and what each side wants
paragraphs: Charles B. Klein argued for Hikma and other the sides that brought the case. Malcolm L. Stewart argued for the United States, supporting the sides that brought the case as amicus. Michael R. Huston argued for Amarin, the the opposing side. the sides that brought the case asked the Court to reverse the decision below.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the sides that brought the case argue that statements consistent with skinny-label use cannot count as active inducement. They say section 271(b) permits selling dual-use products without active inducement. They also say Hatch-Waxman section viii protects skinny-label generics from an infringing use.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 5, lines 23-9

sections.heading: What each side says, continued
paragraphs: the sides that brought the case add that Amarin's complaint is not plausible under Twombly and Iqbal. Those standards mean a complaint must show a plausible claim, not just guesses. the sides that brought the case say obvious alternative explanations defeat plausibility at the pleading stage. They also dispute the opposing sides' claimed new discovery evidence of inducement intent.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The case tests how far patent inducement liability reaches into generic drug communications. It also tests the pleading standard for these claims. The Hatch-Waxman compromise for skinny-label generics sits in the background. The outcome could shape what generic makers may say publicly.
